questions.q: A residual is defined as actual − predicted. A flat sold for ₹80 lakh and the model predicted ₹72 lakh. What does the residual of +8 tell you?
options: The model predicted too high
The model predicted too low
The model's error was 8%
The model was 8 times too low
questions.why: A positive residual means the actual value exceeded the prediction, so the model under-predicted by ₹8 lakh. Reading the sign the other way round is a common slip; the error is in lakh, not percent.

questions.q: Actual values are 50, 60 and 70; predictions are 55, 58 and 80. What is the MAE?
options: About 5.67
About −4.33
About 6.56
questions.why: Errors are −5, +2, −10; absolute errors 5, 2, 10; MAE = 17 / 3 ≈ **5.67**. −4.33 is the mean signed error, where misses in opposite directions cancel; 6.56 is the RMSE; 17 forgets to divide by 3.

questions.q: For the same data (actual 50, 60, 70; predicted 55, 58, 80), what is R²?
questions.why: Model squared errors: 25 + 4 + 100 = 129. A lazy model predicting the mean (60) has 100 + 0 + 100 = 200. R² = 1 − 129 / 200 = **0.355**. 0.645 is 129 / 200 itself, the share of lazy error that remains, not the share removed.

questions.q: A demand model has MAE = 12 units and RMSE = 30 units. What does the large gap suggest?
options: The model is biased upwards
The model is excellent, since MAE is small
The two metrics were computed on different data
Most misses are modest, but a few are very large, because RMSE punishes big misses heavily
questions.why: RMSE squares the misses before averaging, so a handful of large errors inflate it far above MAE. If all misses were similar in size, the two would be close. The gap says nothing about direction (bias); look at the mean signed error for that.

questions.q: Some products have weeks with zero sales. Why is MAPE a poor choice here?
options: MAPE cannot handle negative errors
MAPE only works for classification
MAPE is always larger than RMSE
MAPE divides each miss by the actual value, so it is undefined or explodes when actuals are zero or tiny; WAPE (total absolute error ÷ total actual) avoids this
questions.why: Percentage errors need a non-zero denominator. A miss of 3 units on an actual of 0 gives an infinite percentage. WAPE divides once by the total, so small individual actuals cannot dominate.

questions.q: A price model scores R² = −0.2 on the test set. What does that mean?
options: A calculation error, because R² cannot be negative
The model does worse than simply predicting the average price for every flat
The model explains 20% of the variation
The model is slightly better than the average
questions.why: R² compares the model's squared errors with those of a lazy mean predictor. A negative value means the model's errors are larger. Believing R² is bounded between 0 and 1 is a common misconception; on new data it can go below zero.

questions.q: Three products: actual sales 40, 10, 50; forecasts 30, 20, 45. What are the WAPE and the MAPE?
options: WAPE 25%, MAPE 45%
WAPE 45%, MAPE 25%
WAPE 25%, MAPE 25%
WAPE 8.3%, MAPE 45%
questions.why: Absolute misses 10, 10, 5 total 25; actuals total 100, so WAPE = **25%**. Percentage misses are 25%, 100% and 10%, so MAPE = 135 / 3 = **45%**. The small product (actual 10) inflates MAPE; WAPE weights each product by its size. 8.3% divides the average miss by the total instead of the total miss.

questions.q: Interview: "How do you choose between MAE and RMSE for a forecasting model?" Which answer is best?
options: Always use RMSE, because it is what models minimise
Use whichever gives the smaller number

Ask how errors cost money: if a miss of 20 is about twice as bad as a miss of 10, use MAE; if one large miss (a stock-out, an under-reserved claim) is much worse than several small ones, use RMSE. Report it alongside a naive baseline
Always use R², because it is unit-free
questions.why: The best metric mirrors the business cost of errors. Choosing the metric that looks smaller is a reporting trick, not an evaluation. R² is handy for comparing models on the same data but says nothing about error size in business units.
